title: "Usage"

## Installation

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.add(url = "https://github.com/fesmc/PlasticIceSheet.jl")
```

The core package depends only on the standard libraries `LinearAlgebra` and `SparseArrays`.
Reverse-mode differentiation and NetCDF I/O are loaded on demand through package extensions
(below).

## Solving

```julia
using PlasticIceSheet

z_s, H = solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)
```

| argument | meaning |
|---|---|
| `z_b` | bed elevation $z_b$ (m), `nx × ny` matrix |
| `τ_b` | basal shear stress (Pa), scalar or field |
| `mask` | `true` where grounded ice exists; the margin is the mask boundary |
| `dx`, `dy` | grid spacings (m) |

Returns `(z_s, H)`, the surface elevation and thickness. Ice-free cells have `H = 0` and
`z_s = z_b`. Pad the mask with at least one ice-free cell, since an ice region without an
ice-free cell is unreachable (it is returned with `H = 0` and a warning).

Keyword options (see the `solve` docstring for the rest):

- `mode`: `:surface` (default) solves the plastic surface equation directly over any bed
  relief, in one sweep solve. `:flat` solves the flat-bed eikonal for $H^2$ and drapes it on
  the bed; it is the cheapest mode and equals `:surface` on a flat bed. `:full` adds the bed
  gradient to the $H^2$ equation by a damped fixed point (`n_outer`, `outer_tol`, `relax`);
  it is kept for comparison and does not converge on rough real beds
  ([Algorithms §3](algorithms.qmd#sec-full)).
- `z_ss`: sea level (m), scalar or field. Marine margins are grounded at the flotation
  thickness $(\rho_w/\rho_i)\max(z_{ss} - z_b, 0)$.
- `margin`: where the margin lies between an ice cell and its ice-free neighbour. `:face`
  (default) puts it on the cell face, `:centre` on the ice-free cell centre (the behaviour
  before v0.2), and a field `margin_frac` ∈ [0, 1) gives its distance from the ice-free cell
  centre as a fraction of the spacing ([Algorithms §6](algorithms.qmd#sec-margin)).
- `params`: a `PlasticParams` with the densities `ρ_i`, `ρ_w`, gravity `g` and the
  thickness floor `H_min`.

A margin known as a signed distance (m, positive in the ice) converts to `margin_frac`:

```julia
frac = margin_frac_from_sdist(sdist, mask, dx, dy)
z_s, H = solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy, margin = frac)
```

On a 300 × 300 grid a `:surface` solve takes about 6 ms, `:flat` about 3 ms and a converging
`:full` solve about 1 s.

### Coulomb yield law

A Coulomb yield law, $\tau_b = \mu N_\text{eff}(H)$, replaces the prescribed $\tau_b$
([Algorithms §2](algorithms.qmd#sec-coulomb)):

```julia
law = CoulombYield(μ; H_N = 1000.0, p = 1.0, δ = 0.05)   # μ scalar or field
z_s, H = solve(z_b, law, mask; dx, dy, z_ss)            # mode = :surface only
τ_b = coulomb_taub(H, z_b, mask, law; z_ss)             # the law's τ_b at H
```

`H_N` (m) caps the effective pressure and `δ ∈ (0, 1]` floors it at flotation; the floor
keeps the solution unique and continuous in the bed and sea level. Forward-mode derivatives
with respect to `μ` work; `differentiable_thickness` does not take the law.

### Diagnostics

```julia
ice_volume(H, dx, dy)                          # m³
ice_area(mask, dx, dy)                         # m²
surface_misfit(z_s, z_s_obs, mask)             # mean-squared surface misfit over ice
r = stress_residual(z_s, z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)   # |ρ_i g H |∇z_s| − τ_b| / τ_b per cell
```

`stress_residual` checks how well a geometry satisfies the plastic stress balance, in any mode.
It is a cell-centred measure and is of order 1 at the first ice cell (the one-sided slope of
a square-root profile), so read it away from the margin. On a 300 m bed bump the median over
the interior is about 0.04 for `:surface` and 0.5 for `:flat`.

## Velocity and surface mass balance

The plastic solve returns only geometry. A DIVA closure on the fixed geometry recovers a
depth-averaged velocity and a first-order SMB ([Algorithms §8](algorithms.qmd#sec-closures)).
Pick a rheology and a sliding law:

```julia
rheology = GlenRheology(A = 1.0e-16, n = 3.0)            # isothermal Glen, per year
sliding  = WeertmanSliding(β = 1.0e4, m = 3.0)           # or LinearSliding(β),
                                                         # RegularizedCoulomb(C, u_0, m; u_max)
```

The coefficient (`β`, or `C` for `RegularizedCoulomb`) may be a field of the grid's shape.
`RegularizedCoulomb` returns a `NaN` sliding speed where `τ_b ≥ C`, since the bed is at its
Coulomb cap and the speed is undetermined. With a finite speed cap `u_max`, the speed is
`min(u_b, u_max)` instead, and `u_max` at the cap.

### Closure B: velocity, then implied SMB

```julia
vel = diva_velocity(z_s, H, τ_b, mask, dx, dy; rheology, sliding)
# named tuple: ux, uy, speed, u_b (sliding), u_def (deformation), ex, ey (flow direction)

smb = smb_from_velocity(vel, H, z_s, mask, dx, dy)      # ḃ = ∇·(ūH), MFD operator
```

### Closure A: balance velocity from a prescribed SMB

```julia
bal = balance_velocity(z_s, H, mask, smb, dx, dy)       # named tuple: speed, ux, uy, Q, ...
ib  = implied_basal_velocity(z_s, H, τ_b, mask, smb, dx, dy; rheology)
# ib.u_basal = u_balance − u_def: the basal velocity that geometry and SMB demand
```

`balance_flux` is the exact inverse of `smb_from_velocity`, so routing closure B's SMB back
through closure A recovers closure B's flux to machine precision.

### SMB-driven reconstruction

The dual of `solve` drives the geometry with an SMB (m ice yr⁻¹) instead of a yield stress,
on the same fixed margin ([Algorithms §9](algorithms.qmd#sec-reconstruct)):

```julia
z_s, H = diva_reconstruct(z_b, mask, smb, dx, dy; rheology, sliding, z_ss)
```

The default `method = :steady` solves steady mass conservation $\nabla\cdot\mathbf q = \dot b$
with $H \ge 0$ directly. Mask cells where ablation exceeds the inflow end ice-free. It stops
when the residual falls below `res_tol` (m yr⁻¹) and warns otherwise. On Greenland at 16 km
(`examples/reconstruct_greenland.jl`) it takes a few seconds.

The implied SMB of this method for a given geometry, with the margin outflow and the surface
velocity of the same closure, is:

```julia
o = smb_flux_divergence(z_b, H, mask, dx, dy; rheology, sliding, z_ss, τ_cap = τ_b)
# named tuple: smb, q_land, q_marine (outflow per margin cell), us_x, us_y
```

The geometry `H` is a root of the steady problem forced by `o.smb`. `τ_cap` (optional) caps
the driving stress of the fluxes, since a plastic bed carries at most its yield stress.

`method = :routing` keeps the earlier iteration (route the SMB, invert the flux law for the
driving stress, plastic sweep, under-relax). It is stable only for `relax` below roughly
slope × Δx / H, i.e., 0.003–0.04 in tests, and is kept for comparison.

## Inverting for $\tau_b$

The solver is differentiable with respect to $\tau_b$
([Algorithms §7](algorithms.qmd#sec-ad)).

### Forward mode: scalar or low-dimensional $\tau_b$

```julia
using ForwardDiff
loss(τ_b) = surface_misfit(first(solve(z_b, τ_b, mask; dx, dy)), z_s_obs, mask)
g = ForwardDiff.derivative(loss, 1.0e5)
```

### Reverse mode: a full per-cell $\tau_b$ field

Load the extension triggers, then differentiate `differentiable_thickness` with any
reverse-mode AD:

```julia
using ImplicitDifferentiation, ADTypes, ForwardDiff, Zygote

loss(τ_b) = surface_misfit(differentiable_thickness(τ_b, z_b, mask; dx, dy) .+ z_b, z_s_obs, mask)
g = Zygote.gradient(loss, τ_b)[1]      # gradient with respect to the whole τ_b field
```

`differentiable_thickness` takes the same `mode`, `z_ss` and `margin` keywords as `solve`.
The default reverse-mode linear solver is direct, which is robust for modest grids. For very
large fields, pass an iterative solver (see the `differentiable_thickness` docstring).

[`examples/invert_tau.jl`](https://github.com/fesmc/PlasticIceSheet.jl/blob/main/examples/invert_tau.jl)
recovers a spatially varying $\tau_b$ from an observed surface with Adam, and
[Inversion](inversion.qmd) covers the parameterizations of $\tau_b$ on real data.

## NetCDF I/O

```julia
using NCDatasets

inp = load_plastic_inputs("inputs.nc")             # (; z_b, τ_b, mask, dx, dy, x, y)
z_s, H = solve(inp.z_b, inp.τ_b, inp.mask; inp.dx, inp.dy)
save_reconstruction("out.nc", z_s, H; x = inp.x, y = inp.y)
```

## Examples

The scripts in
[`examples/`](https://github.com/fesmc/PlasticIceSheet.jl/tree/main/examples) run with
`julia --project=examples examples/<script>.jl`. The Greenland scripts read the GRL-16KM or
GRL-32KM grids from an `examples/ice_data` directory (not included).

| script | content |
|---|---|
| `invert_tau.jl` | synthetic per-cell $\tau_b$ recovery with Adam (reverse mode) |
| `invert_taub_greenland.jl` | $\tau_b$ inversion on Greenland, tiled or per-cell (`METHOD`) |
| `invert_taub_sweep_greenland.jl` | rmse against the number of tiles |
| `smb_from_velocity_greenland.jl` | implied SMB from observed velocity and thickness, against the climate SMB |
| `reconstruct_greenland.jl` | SMB-driven reconstruction from the MAR SMB, with balance velocity |

## Caveats

- The geometry is steady state only. It is biased thick where the real ice was streaming
  or otherwise dynamic, since the plastic assumption sees no reduced driving stress there.
- $\tau_b$ carries essentially all of the uncertainty. For a first guess a constant
  (about 50–100 kPa) or a bed-keyed value is reasonable, but the result is not a constrained
  reconstruction.
- `:surface` and `:flat` are first-order accurate. At 10–30 km the margin position and
  the coarse inputs change the ice volume by several percent
  ([Algorithms §6](algorithms.qmd#sec-margin)).

## Fortran library

[PlasticIceSheet](https://github.com/fesmc/PlasticIceSheet) is a dependency-free Fortran
port of the forward solver, the Coulomb yield law and the closures (`libplastic.a`), for
coupling into Fortran models. It uses the same schemes (results were verified bit-identical
against v0.1) and adds a warm start, OpenMP parallelism and a joint inversion of speed and
SMB. The $\tau_b$
inversion and the AD extension remain Julia-only.
